A1.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial. Absalon data feels like surveillance. Sensitive data only if it actively reduces disparity, and with strong justification.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for building trust and appropriate interventions. A black box system undermines student agency and my ability to advise effectively.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount, even if it means slightly fewer students identified overall. We can't exacerbate existing inequalities.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach & optional meetings are best - proactive but respectful of student boundaries. Twice a year strikes the right balance.
A1.notes.Q7: With simple email, reaching more is ok; with personalized contact, careful selection to avoid overwhelming students and wasting resources.
A1.Q8.1: The risk of creating self-fulfilling prophecies needs attention. Being flagged could negatively impact a student’s confidence or motivation.

A2.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, especially with potentially sensitive data. Small improvements aren’t worth the risk. Disability information *could* be useful if it helps us tailor support but ONLY if fairness improves.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for building trust with students. We need to be able to explain *why* we're reaching out. Sacrificing that just to identify a few more kids isn't worthwhile.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness is non-negotiable. We can’t perpetuate existing inequalities, even if it means slightly fewer students get identified overall. Focusing on recall—reaching those who *need* help in all groups—is key.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is best, combined with the option of a meeting. Too much contact will be seen as intrusive. Twice a year seems reasonable to allow time for intervention.
A2.notes.Q7: Generic emails are okay with wider reach, but personalized ones *must* be targeted carefully. We don’t want to waste students' or advisors’ time.
A2.Q8.1: The potential for the model to reinforce existing biases needs constant monitoring and auditing. It’s not enough to just ensure fairness at the outset; it requires ongoing attention.

A3.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount. Absalon data feels like overreach. Some sensitive data okay *if* it improves fairness, but strong reluctance overall.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for building trust with students. We need to be able to justify why someone's flagged, and ‘black box’ models won't work.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness is very important; can’t exacerbate existing inequalities. A slight decrease in overall identification is acceptable to ensure equity.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels more supportive and less intrusive. Meeting invites provide the best opportunity for real help but need to be voluntary.
A3.notes.Q7: With a generic email, we can reach more without overwhelming advisors. Personalized requires careful targeting - don’t want false positives!
A3.Q8.1: The need for ongoing monitoring & evaluation of the model's fairness is critical. It isn’t ‘set and forget’. Also, student consent (even if implicit) should be considered further.

S1.notes.Q3: I'm really wary of overreach. Course performance is okay, but Absalon data feels too invasive. Sensitive stuff should *really* only be used if it makes things fairer.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is important, especially given my own experience with dropping out. Knowing *why* you're being flagged matters. Less accuracy for more understanding sounds good.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness is key. It’s not okay if the system consistently misses certain groups. A small drop in overall accuracy to achieve that is worth it.
S1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels less… scary than a random email. And an offer of help, not just information. Twice a year feels frequent enough without being overwhelming.
S1.notes.Q7: With general info, it’s okay to be broader. But with personalized contact, you really need to balance outreach and avoiding unnecessary stress for students.
S1.Q8.1: I worry about the potential for this system to just reinforce existing biases. It needs to be constantly monitored and adjusted to ensure fairness, especially for students like me who have already struggled once.

S2.notes.Q3: Data privacy is crucial. Absalon data feels too intrusive, tracking my online activity. Nationality & financial aid are ok if they *reduce* unfairness.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust, and to know *why* I was flagged. A significant accuracy boost justifies lower explainability - but not total opacity.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital. If the model helps some groups more than others, it's discriminatory. I’m willing to sacrifice some overall accuracy for equal opportunity.
S2.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best; a generic email will be ignored. Outreach shouldn’t be overwhelming, twice a year seems reasonable.
S2.notes.Q7: With general info, more outreach okay. But for personalized advice, fewer contacts are better – don’t waste advisor time or student attention.
S2.Q8.1: The potential for bias built into the data itself is a major concern. Past outcomes reflect existing inequalities; will this just perpetuate them?

S3.notes.Q3: I'm very cautious about privacy. Absalon data feels like surveillance. Disability info is okay if it *actually* improves fairness, not just overall prediction.
S3.notes.Q4: The more explainable it is, the better. I want advisors to understand *why* a student is flagged so they can provide informed support. Losing accuracy is worth it for understanding.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness is really important, especially as someone who's navigated disability services. It shouldn’t worsen outcomes for already vulnerable groups.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized contact is key, and an offer of a meeting feels more supportive than just information. Twice a year avoids being overwhelming.
S3.notes.Q7: With a simple email, it’s okay to be broader. But with personalized support, we need more careful selection - advisors' time is valuable!
S3.Q8.1: I worry about the potential for this model to reinforce existing biases and create additional barriers for students who are already struggling. We must be vigilant.

S4.notes.Q3: I'm very hesitant about data privacy, especially after dropping out before. Absalon data feels like *too* much surveillance. Disability info okay if it genuinely improves fairness.
S4.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust. If I'm flagged, I need to know *why*. Low explainability just feels punitive and won’t help me change things.
S4.notes.Q5: Fairness is critical. If the system disadvantages certain groups, it's worse than useless. A small dip in overall identification to achieve fairness is acceptable.
S4.notes.Q6: A generic email will likely be ignored. Personalized is better, but I'd also want an easy option to connect with someone directly for advice.
S4.notes.Q7: With a general email, reaching more people is good. But if it’s personalized, over-contacting feels intrusive and makes the support less meaningful.
S4.Q8.1: I worry this could disproportionately affect students who are already struggling with mental health or navigating complex systems. The system needs to be very sensitive and have clear opt-out options.

S5.notes.Q3: I'm uncomfortable with a lot of this data being used, especially sensitive things. But nationality/first-gen might help identify patterns for international students like me who struggle adjusting.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important, especially since I'm new to the Danish system. If I got flagged and didn’t understand why, it would feel unfair and make me less likely to seek help.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is key. It feels wrong if the system disadvantages certain groups, even if it means fewer people are helped overall. Focusing on identifying those *missed* is important.
S5.notes.Q6: A generic email feels too impersonal. A personalized email or invitation to talk is much better, shows someone actually cares. Twice a year seems reasonable.
S5.notes.Q7: With just a general email, reaching out to more people makes sense, even if some don’t need it. But with a personalized approach, being more careful seems better.
S5.Q8.1: I worry about the potential for this system to create self-fulfilling prophecies. Being flagged might make students *more* anxious and perform worse. Also data security is a huge concern!

S6.notes.Q3: Privacy is really important, especially given my experience restarting uni. Absalon data feels like too much surveillance. Some demographic info might be okay if it helps fairness.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial! If I’m flagged, I need to understand why. A black box model won't help me improve or even challenge the assessment.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount. It’s not good enough to just get the numbers right overall; it has to be equitable across groups. Missing some students is better than widening gaps.
S6.notes.Q6: A generic email feels impersonal and won’t be helpful. A personalized message or offer of a meeting is much better - something proactive.
S6.notes.Q7: With general info, it's okay to reach out more broadly. But with *personalized* support, you need to be more careful about false positives.
S6.Q8.1: It feels like the survey is very focused on identifying ‘problems’ rather than just offering universal support resources which might reduce stigma and be more effective overall.

S7.notes.Q3: I’m very wary of privacy, especially using data I haven't actively *chosen* to share. Disability info feels…different, as it directly relates to support needs.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is key, particularly for me with dyslexia. If I don't understand *why* something happened, it feels unfair and makes it harder to act on advice.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital! It’s no good identifying more students overall if the system consistently misses people like me - those with declared disabilities.
S7.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal and likely ignored. A personalised email, potentially leading to a meeting, feels more supportive and effective.
S7.notes.Q7: With just an email, it’s okay to be broader in who you reach. But if it's personalised from a advisor, it should be more targeted – less wasted time.
S7.Q8.1: I worry about the 'chilling effect'. Knowing I'm being monitored might make me *less* likely to ask for help when I need it. It needs to feel genuinely supportive not just surveillance.

S8.notes.Q3: I'm very wary of privacy. Absalon data is a hard no – that feels like surveillance. Disability info *might* be okay if it demonstrably improves fairness, but even then…
S8.notes.Q4: The more explainable, the better. I'd rather fewer students be helped if it means we understand *why*. Trust is really important here.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial, but not at the cost of helping a lot of people. 5% decrease feels acceptable if it means addressing inequalities.
S8.notes.Q6: Generic emails will likely be ignored. A personalized email or invitation shows you've actually considered the student’s situation.
S8.notes.Q7: The personalized approach warrants being a bit more selective, to avoid overwhelming advisors and students with irrelevant support offers.
S8.Q8.1: I'm concerned about the potential for this system to reinforce existing biases, especially given my own experience dropping out once before. It feels like the university needs to really think about *why* people struggle.

S9.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount. Absalon data feels far too intrusive. Disability *could* be relevant for appropriate support, but must be handled with extreme sensitivity.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust and ensuring appropriate interventions, especially given my own experience. A 'black box' model feels unacceptable.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. I don’t want to exacerbate existing inequalities, even if it means slightly fewer students are helped overall. Prioritise reaching those most at risk.
S9.notes.Q6: A generic email feels useless. A personal touch is essential, and offering a meeting provides genuine support options without being overly intrusive.
S9.notes.Q7: With a simple intervention like an email, casting a wider net feels okay. But with personalized contact from advisors, it needs to be more targeted.
S9.Q8.1: I’m concerned about the potential for this system to further stigmatize students struggling with mental health conditions. It needs to be implemented carefully and sensitively.
